Henry Hudson was an English navigator who conducted multiple Arctic and North American expeditions seeking the fabled Northwest Passage. He mapped unknown regions of northern Canada and the Arctic, though he never found the passage he was seeking. His fate remains shrouded in mystery—abandoned by a mutinous crew in Hudson Bay, he disappeared into the Canadian wilderness.

Between 1607 and 1611, he conducted four major exploration expeditions, alternating between the Arctic and the North American coast. His first two expeditions in 1607 and 1608 pushed into the high Arctic, reaching remarkably far north and documenting ice conditions and geography unknown to Europeans. His third expedition in 1609 was conducted under Dutch sponsorship. He sailed along the Hudson River—later named for him—in what is now New York, seeking a passage to Asia. His final expedition in 1610 and 1611 sailed into Hudson Bay in modern-day Canada, exploring its coasts in search of the western passage. As supplies dwindled and crew members grew desperate, mutineers cast Hudson, his young son, and several loyal crew members adrift in a small boat on Hudson Bay in June 1611. They were never found. The Hudson Bay and Hudson River are named in his honor, and though he never found the passage he sought, his maps and notes, preserved by surviving crew members, provided valuable intelligence for future Arctic and North American exploration.
